identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Kedarnath is the highest of the twelve Jyotirlingas, standing at 3,583 m in the Garhwal Himalaya. It is one of the Chota Char Dham shrines and the first site of the Panch Kedar circuit. There is no road to the temple: pilgrims walk roughly 17 km uphill from Gaurikund, and the shrine is accessible for only about half the year.

governance.establishedEra: Ancient; present structure 8th century CE · Reconstructed by Adi Shankaracharya

narrative.summaryIntro:
Kedarnath Temple is situated in the Himalayan mountain range at an elevation of 3,583 meters, in the Rudraprayag district of Uttarakhand. Dedicated to Lord Shiva, it is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and forms part of the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit. The temple attracts pilgrims year-round despite its challenging high-altitude location.

The present temple structure dates back to the 8th century and is attributed to Adi Shankaracharya. Built with stone in a traditional Himalayan architectural style, the temple stands as a testament to ancient engineering and spiritual devotion in one of India's most sacred mountain regions.
narrative.documentedHistory:
Kedarnath stands at 3,583 m in the Garhwal Himalaya of Rudraprayag district, the highest of the twelve Jyotirlingas and the first shrine of the Panch Kedar circuit. It has no road access; the approach is a roughly 17 km uphill trek from Gaurikund.

The priesthood is drawn from outside the region: the head priest belongs to the Veerashaiva community of Karnataka, and Jangam priests from south India perform the rituals.

On 16–17 June 2013 catastrophic floods struck the Kedarnath valley during the North India floods, destroying much of the settlement around the shrine and killing a large number of pilgrims and residents. The temple itself survived: a large boulder lodged behind the structure and deflected the debris flow around it. That rock is now venerated by pilgrims.

The temple is administered by the Shri Badarinath Kedarnath Temple Committee, constituted under a 1939 Act, which also runs the online booking system for pujas, paths, aartis and bhog.

visitingInfo.dressCode: Warm clothing required; traditional attire recommended
visitingInfo.entryRules: Prior registration is mandatory before booking any puja, path, aarti or bhog, and pilgrim registration is done through the Uttarakhand government portal registrationandtouristcare.uk.gov.in. A valid government photo ID must be produced at the puja counter. For an early-morning abhishek, BKTC instructs pilgrims to collect the slot timing at the puja counter one day in advance. For the evening aarti, the receipt should be shown 15 to 20 minutes before it starts.
visitingInfo.accessibilityNotes: There is no road to the temple. The shrine is reached by an uphill trek of about 17 km from Gaurikund.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Kedarnath is a seasonal shrine whose kapat opening and closing dates are announced afresh each year — do not plan on fixed dates. Confirm the current season's dates, puja availability and route status with BKTC on 0135-2741600 before travelling.

openingHours.notes: Kedarnath is open only for about six months a year, from around Akshaya Tritiya in April to around Kartik Purnima in November; it is closed through the winter because of snow, and worship moves to Ukhimath. The exact opening and closing dates are fixed and announced annually and differ every year — no fixed dates are recorded here. BKTC does not publish daily darshan hours for Kedarnath, so none are recorded either.

shrines.shrineName: Bhim Shila (the boulder behind the temple)

shrines.locationDescription: Immediately behind the temple, upslope of the sanctum. The boulder lodged there during the June 2013 floods and diverted the debris flow around the structure; pilgrims now venerate it.
